welcome.title: Welcome to PTSD Help
welcome.description: This app is designed to support trauma survivors. Please note that it cannot provide medical diagnosis or treatment - these services can only be provided by healthcare professionals. But it can help you learn more about PTSD and manage your symptoms, by providing you with the necessary tools and information for managing the distress that trauma can cause.

personalize.l2: Your favorite tools for managing stress
personalize.modify_preferences: You can always modify your preferences later from the settings menu.

distress-meter.title: What's your current level of distress?
distress-meter.scale: {{min}} means no distress, {{max}} is the worst
distress-meter.subtitle: Tap on the '+' and '-' arrows to indicate how you are feeling.
distress-meter.info: Distress can include anger, sadness, fear, pain, stress, worry, or any negative feeling you experience. Evaluate your level of distress before and after using a support tool to figure out which tools work best for you.

info-levels.high: 10 = the highest level of distress you can imagine

distress-meter.info-pre: Distress can include anger, sadness, fear, pain, stress, worry, or any negative feeling you experience. Evaluate your level of distress before and after using a support tool to figure out which tools work best for you.
distress-meter.info-post: You've done a good job completing this tool, now you will evaluate your level of distress on a scale from 0 to 10 to see if there has been a decrease in your discomfort level.

high-distress.text: This is a very high level of distress. It would be good to get help as soon as possible. Would you like to talk to someone now?

actions.help: No, continue to the support tool
actions.talk: Yes, I want to talk to someone

increased.title: Distress increased
increased.description:
It seems that after {{toolName}} you are actually more distressed. It may be good to remember for the future, since you shouldn't do things that don't work for you. But remember, some of these tools need time or practice to work or can only improve certain types of problems, so don't remove it yet. 

As you're still distressed, you may want to try another tool.

decreased.title: Distress decreased
decreased.description:
Great! It seems that {{toolName}} has reduced your distress level. Try to remember this tool. Anything that works for you once can work again! 

If a tool continues to work for you, you may want to mark it as a favorite by pressing the heart icon the next time this tool is offered. This way, it will be more likely to show up again. The tool will also be saved in 'Favorites'.

unchanged.title: Distress unchanged
unchanged.description:
OK, it seems that after {{toolName}} you have the same amount of stress. It may be enough for you – after all, nothing has gotten worse! – or maybe you expected a bigger improvement. But don't forget, some of these tools need time or practice to work or can only improve certain types of problems, so don't remove it yet. 

If you want, you can safely try another tool now.

privacy-policy.title: Privacy policy
privacy-policy.content:
When you use a Code for Romania mobile app, no data that could be used to identify you is sent to Code for Romania or third parties. Any information that you enter into the app, such as names, phone numbers, addresses, images, or music, cannot be accessed, stored, or shared by Code for Romania. Code for Romania mobile apps do collect anonymous information about how people use the app. It is only used to improve how well the app works. We can see what sections of the app people visit, for example. We often use this information to correct technical problems in the apps. This information cannot be linked to any personal information about you and will never be shared with a third party. If you would like to turn off sending this anonymous usage information, go to the Settings menu, look for “Anonymous Usage Data,” and flip the switch to the “off” setting.

Code for Romania uses some software analysis tools to help identify and prevent app problems. Code for Romania mobile apps do not share personal or identifying information with any of the partners of this tool. In using a Code for Romania mobile app, it is your responsibility to protect any information in the app once it is installed on your device. Setting a passcode on your device is recommended to help keep your information safe.

content.content: People who have experienced traumatic events have different experiences as they recover, but the following problems are common and occur after trauma. You may experience some, all or none of the following problems.

content: Trauma memories: you frequently have upsetting thoughts or memories about the trauma, feel like it's happening again, and/or feel very stressed when reminded of it.
Avoiding reminders: You make an effort to avoid thoughts, feelings, conversations, places, or people that remind you of the trauma.
Disconnected from people: You feel distant from others, have difficulty feeling love and/or feel alienated and lonely.
Disconnected from reality: You feel disconnected from the world, from other people or from yourself, "in a fog," "in a dream," "out of body," or as if things seem unreal.
Sad / Hopeless: You feel sad, hopeless or depressed, have no interest in activities that used to be pleasurable or just in life in general, feel a sense of meaninglessness and/or despair.
Worried / Anxious: You startle easily and are easily frightened, are tense and "on guard" most of the time.
Angry: You are easily irritated, have outbursts of anger, feelings of distrust.
Sleep problems: You have trouble falling asleep and/or staying asleep, have nightmares and may wake up sweating.

content.content: The 'Change your perspective' tool gives you reminders that can offer you hope and confidence.

We all have a constant stream of thoughts passing through our minds - this is called self-talk. Negative self-talk, such as believing things are terrible or the worst will happen, can stress your body and keep you on alert all the time.
These positive self-talk reminders give you something to hold onto; they can help you think more realistically and may even help you manage situations more effectively.

When facing life's challenges, it can help to seek support from people you know and trust, or just to relax in the presence of others. People who receive support from friends and relatives face fewer physical and emotional symptoms of stress than those who do not.
Choose people in your life whom you can contact when you need support. Friends, family, coworkers and even healthcare providers can be added to your personal contact list.

This activity will guide you through a short exercise in which you breathe more slowly and deeply to help you relax. Slow, deep breathing helps balance carbon dioxide and oxygen in your blood. This calms your nervous system, creating a "relaxation response." Deep breathing exercises can help manage stress and insomnia, focus your mind, and improve health.

These exercises are simple strategies to distract yourself and detach from intense emotional pain or, on the other hand, to help you reconnect with your body or self if you feel disconnected, numb, "foggy" or detached.

These strategies include tips to fall asleep as quickly as possible and also tips for managing insomnia so you can more easily fall asleep regularly. People who have experienced trauma often have trouble falling or staying asleep, or struggle with nightmares. These strategies, along with some of the relaxation exercises in this app, can help you relax and sleep better.
These quotes can offer inspiration and new perspectives for trauma survivors.

If you can do something to actively change the situation affecting your mood and it's safe to do so, now is a good time to start. Especially if you feel disappointed, it may be hard to feel motivated to do things that would usually be fun or give you a sense of fulfillment. However, research shows that making the effort to do these things even when you don't feel like it can improve your mood.

This exercise guides you, either sitting comfortably or lying down, through tensing and relaxing a sequence of muscle groups. This allows your muscles to relax more deeply than usual. This exercise can help lower heart rate and blood pressure, slow your breathing, decrease muscular tension, and promote clear thinking.

This exercise is also great because, over time, you can train yourself to truly know how your muscles feel when tense and how they feel when relaxed. Then, when you recognize your muscles are tense or becoming tense, you can relax them because you have trained yourself to know what relaxed muscles feel like.

When something has triggered your traumatic memory, your mind and body behave as if the traumatic experience is happening now. These immediate, automatic reactions are adaptive and useful during the real event, since they keep you safe in dangerous situations. But now, your automatic reactions to triggers are no longer helpful, since at home, you're in no real danger.

Use the RID tool to stay focused and deal with triggers. Remember that triggers confuse your brain and body, making you believe you're back in the original situation. It's important to clear up this confusion in order to manage your responses.

RID has three steps: The first step, R in RID, is to Relax or calm yourself. The second step is to Identify what is triggering you and how it is different from your original trauma. And the third step, D in RID, is to Decide how to respond to the trigger. Doing these three things when you are triggered can be very helpful.

This exercise helps you take a break from a worsening situation before you (or someone else) do something you regret. A timeout is a break taken during a conflict (often 10-15 minutes) that helps people manage their anger, so they can resolve conflicts more effectively. The timeout exercise provides more instructions and guidance on how and when to take a timeout and what to do to help you calm down while on your own.

You can learn to interrupt unhelpful thoughts that upset you before you do or say something you regret. It's important to break your train of thought and say a phrase to yourself in that tense moment to counteract angry thoughts before you get into trouble. You can also use thought shifting to prepare before entering a risky situation.
Sometimes it's helpful to picture something at the same time or repeat the phrase to yourself a few times.

There isn't a single correct thing to say when interrupting unhelpful angry thoughts. Thought shifting is most helpful when what you say is meaningful to you. With practice, you can find phrases that work well for you.
